events.text: The seat of the domain you were born heir to has been kept, through ages, by deputies who dust it and do not sit. When you walk in, they all stand. Nobody speaks. A very old deputy brings you the key, which is warm, and says in a small voice that they had stopped expecting anyone and had kept the dusting anyway.

effects.log: You thank the deputies by name, all forty, which takes an hour. By the end they are standing a little straighter, and one is crying into a sleeve.
You sit down at once, without ceremony. The seat takes your weight as if it had been waiting for exactly that, and the deputies exhale as one.

choices.text: Ask what the domain has needed

effects.log: You ask what the domain has needed these ages. The list is long, and written very small, and you read every line before you sit.

events.text: In the domain you were born heir to, the first thing you find is a drawer in the seat, and in it a child's drawing of your parent, done by you, in a crayon of ground chalk, on the back of a prayer. It has been kept flat for ages. Under it, in your parent's hand, one line: if you ever sit here, you are forgiven for being late.

choices.text: Pin the drawing to the wall

effects.log: You pin the drawing to the wall behind the seat. Visiting gods ask about it. You tell them it is a map, which is nearly true.

choices.text: Put it back in the drawer

effects.log: You put it back in the drawer, and close it gently. Some things are best kept where they have been kept.

choices.text: Write an answer under the line

effects.log: You write an answer under the line, in a hand much larger than the first. It is only one word. It is sufficient.

events.text: Worshippers of the domain have been praying to an empty seat for ages, and the prayers have gathered like leaves in a corner. When you sit, they all arrive at once. It is a flood, a thousand small requests at the same instant, and you gasp, and a deputy runs forward with a cup of cold dew and a look of practised sympathy.

choices.text: Take them one by one, all night

effects.log: You take them one by one, all night, as they come. By dawn you are hoarse and you know your worshippers better than any god in the Halls.
You answer the oldest prayers first, the ones that waited longest. There are tears, in distant villages, over small things that finally came right.

choices.text: Sort them by what they need most

effects.log: You sort them by need, with the deputies, into three heaps. It is cold, and effective, and you sleep like a stone.

events.text: A god who sat beside your parent in the old councils comes to the domain's gate to see you take it. They stand a long time on the threshold with their hands folded, and then say that your parent argued with everybody, lost most of it, and was loved all the same. They say you have the same walk. They are not sure that they mean it as praise.

effects.log: You ask what the arguments were. It takes the afternoon, and by the end you have agreed with half of them, and decided to lose the other half in the same style.

choices.text: Ask them to stay on as advisor

effects.log: You ask them to stay on as advisor. They accept, grumbling, and the domain acquires its first grumbler in an age, which is a sign of health.
You thank them, and say little. They go away looking, if anything, relieved to have been understood by someone who was not going to argue.

events.text: The domain has a custom you did not know about: the new holder must go once around its borders, on foot, before sunset, and speak to whatever they meet. You set out. You meet a lame ox, a quarrel between two weirs, a child with a toy sword, and a very old tree that has been waiting, you are told, for exactly this.

effects.log: You speak to the tree. It says nothing, but the leaves tremble, and a seed falls into your palm, and by the time you reach the gate you are certain it is yours.
You settle the weirs' quarrel, with a sensible compromise about water. By dusk you are home, and by morning the story is round the whole domain.

choices.text: Carry the child the last mile

effects.log: You carry the child the last mile, toy sword and all. It is not the traditional answer, and the domain approves of it so much that it becomes the tradition.

events.text: The seat has an opinion about you. It shows it in small ways: the lamps lean toward you, a draught always finds the right page, the cushion warms exactly when you are tired. It is a presence, patient, old, and amused. At the end of your first year, you hear it say, in a voice like a floorboard settling: you will do. It is the finest thing anyone has said to you.

effects.log: You say thank you, aloud, to an empty room. The lamps flare gently, and the domain, in some sense, adopts you.
You ask what it wants. It answers, over the following ages, in small ways, and every one of them is what a good domain wants and a bad god forgets.

choices.text: Make a mark on the seat's arm

effects.log: You scratch a small mark into the seat's arm, beside the old ones, with your thumbnail. The seat sighs. It has a long row of them, and now one more.

events.text: Before the lineage's pillars of names, you teach {b3_chosen} how to hold a prayer without dropping it: palms open, breath slow, attention turned a little to the left of the sender. {b3_chosen} drops three in a row, and the third makes a tiny lightning. The others of your blood watch from the arches and count.

effects.log: You laugh, and show it again, slower, and {b3_chosen} holds the next one for a full minute. The arches fall quiet in a thoughtful way.
You tell {b3_chosen} to keep the lightning, and learn to aim it. It is the best advice a teacher has ever given, and the worst for the furniture.
You send {b3_chosen} to rest, with a bowl of warm broth. The lesson will keep, you say, and it does, and so does the gratitude.

events.text: A cousin of the lineage, passed over, comes to you in private. They are polite, which is worse than angry. They say that they have served the line for ages, and that {b3_chosen} has served it for decades, and that they would like, if it is not rude, to know what it was that {b3_chosen} did that they did not.

effects.log: You tell the whole truth: nothing but being the right age at the right time, and being asked. The cousin listens, nods slowly, and says it is the first honest answer they have had.

choices.text: Offer the cousin a post of trust

effects.log: You offer the cousin a post of trust, in the house's accounts. They accept, stiffly, and in a century they run the line better than either of you.

choices.text: Say that the choice is made

effects.log: You say that the choice is made, and will not be reopened. It is firm, and cold, and the cousin goes away with the face of someone writing a long letter in their head.

events.text: {b3_chosen} answers a prayer wrongly. It was a small one, the kind of request that comes ten thousand times a season, and the answer was kind and not correct, and a village in the low country got a flood in place of a spring. {b3_chosen} comes to you white with it, and asks, without any attempt at excuse, how bad it is.

choices.text: Go down with {b3_chosen} to mend it

effects.log: You go down with {b3_chosen} to mend it, wading through the silt in your divine slippers. By the next season the village has a new well, and a story about two gods who were wet.

choices.text: Teach the rule, not the remedy

effects.log: You teach the rule behind the mistake, and let {b3_chosen} mend the harm alone. It is harder, and kinder in the end, and takes a century.
You take the blame yourself, in the Halls, with a straight face. {b3_chosen} does not forget it, and does not make that mistake again.

events.text: {b3_chosen} asks you directly, in the quiet of the name-pillars, whether you chose them for love or for use. The question is quiet and absolutely level. It is the kind a god of Fate might ask, and you realise you have asked it of yourself before, and not answered. The pillars wait.

choices.text: Say: for love, and for use

effects.log: You say: for love, and for use, and that you cannot honestly tell which is the larger. {b3_chosen} looks at you for a long time, and says that is the first answer that sounds true.
You say: for love, plainly. It is not the whole truth, but it is a great part, and {b3_chosen}'s face loosens. They never ask again.
You say: for the line. It is honest, and cold, and it opens a distance that takes ages to cross. But it is a clean distance, and {b3_chosen} respects it.

events.text: A rival pantheon sends an envoy to offer {b3_chosen} a seat of their own: more honour, a larger domain, and no need to wait for anyone to die, or be tired, or move over. The envoy lays it out beautifully, in your hearing, with {b3_chosen} watching you rather than them. This is a test of both of you, and everyone knows.

effects.log: You let {b3_chosen} decide, aloud, in front of the envoy. The answer is a polite no, with a joke in it, and you are prouder than you can say.
You outbid the envoy, with a promise of a domain and a title in the line's name. The envoy bows. {b3_chosen} is quiet for a month, and not quite at ease.
You send the envoy home with a gift and a refusal. {b3_chosen} comes to you afterwards and says nothing, and sits down beside you, which is better.

events.text: At the lineage's pillars, a mason asks whether to carve the name of {b3_chosen} beside yours. There is room on the stone, and nothing requires it, and the others of your blood are watching to see what you say. The mason holds the chisel as if it were a sleeping bird.

effects.log: You tell the mason to carve it beside yours, and the chisel falls. The sound goes round the pillars. The others do not breathe. {b3_chosen}, from the arch, does not move.
You tell the mason to carve it one pillar down, where it can rise as it earns. It is the diplomatic answer, and a good one, and {b3_chosen} understands.

choices.text: Leave the stone bare for now

effects.log: You tell the mason to leave the stone bare for now. A bare stone is a promise, and a threat, and the mason leaves, delighted and afraid.

events.text: {b3_chosen} corrects you on a point of divine precedent, in front of three senior gods. It is a small point, and {b3_chosen} is right, and has been very careful to be gentle. The seniors look at you to see what you will do. {b3_chosen} has gone pale. You are about to find out what sort of teacher you have been.

effects.log: You thank {b3_chosen}, aloud, and amend the ruling on the spot. The seniors exchange a look. It is the look of people who have just seen a lineage survive.

choices.text: Say it can be discussed later

effects.log: You say it can be discussed later. It is the diplomatic answer, and you later thank {b3_chosen} in private, and the seniors never learn of it.
You counter with a finer point, and the debate that follows is very good, and the seniors learn more than either of you do. {b3_chosen} grins at you, openly, for the first time.

events.text: One of the lineage who was passed over has been quietly telling the Halls that {b3_chosen} is unready. The charge is half true, and the half that is true is damaging. You hear it first from a servant, who looks at the floor, and then from a god of the Silent Hall, who does not. {b3_chosen} has not heard.

effects.log: You tell {b3_chosen} yourself, that evening. They take it with a long breath and ask how to answer. You say: by being ready. It is not enough, and they know it, and begin.
You quietly confront the talker, in a corridor, with three facts. The talk stops. The talker is not your friend after, and you pay for it, slowly, in small coldnesses.
You say nothing, and let {b3_chosen} earn the answer. It takes a century, and when it comes it is conclusive, and so is the silence of the one who talked.

events.text: {b3_chosen} asks leave to go down among the mortals for a season, and see what it is they pray for. The line has never done this. The elders will call it a risk, and a waste, and a vanity. You remember a time, in a different life, when you wanted to do the same, and did not ask, and went.

choices.text: Grant leave, and give a charm

effects.log: You grant leave, and press a charm into {b3_chosen}'s hand: a pebble you carried once. They come back after a season changed in a way you do not need to ask about.

choices.text: Go down together for a month

effects.log: You go down together for a month, in plain clothes, and eat in a tavern, and listen. It is the best month either of you has had.
You refuse, for the line's peace. It is the sensible answer, and {b3_chosen} accepts it with grace, and a quiet that lasts a hundred years.

events.text: Ages go by, and {b3_chosen} stands in a place you once stood: the head of a table, the foot of a stair, a decision to be made before dusk. You watch from the arches, among the old relatives, and for once you are the one counting. It is humbling, and warm, and has a little jealousy in it, which you decide to admit to.

effects.log: You cheer when the decision comes, aloud, among the old relatives, who are scandalised. {b3_chosen} looks up and, helplessly, grins.
You leave before it is made, so that {b3_chosen} will know they did it alone. You learn the result from a servant, and it is good, and you sit very still.

choices.text: Send word of one small piece of advice

effects.log: You send word of one small piece of advice, on a slip of paper. {b3_chosen} reads it, nods, and puts it in a pocket, where it stays for ages.

events.text: At the new-year supper, the table goes quiet when {b3_chosen} is asked to carve the bird. It is the elder's task, or the heir's, and {b3_chosen} has never held the knife. You see a cousin put down a cup. You see the knife go round. {b3_chosen} takes it with both hands, carefully, and looks at you, not at the bird.

effects.log: You nod, and let {b3_chosen} carve. It is a ruin of a bird and the best you have ever eaten, and the table, at last, applauds.
You carve beside {b3_chosen}, hand over hand. It is slower and neater and nobody in the family forgets the picture.
You take the knife back, gently, with a joke about the poultry. {b3_chosen} is relieved, and a little ashamed to be, and tries again next year.

events.text: Your kin are divided about {b3_chosen}. Half say it is wrong to prefer one child of the house over the rest. The other half say the best should lead. You hear both over the stove, in the same week, from people who have each brought a cake. Neither cake is the problem. The problem is that both are partly right.

effects.log: You tell them {b3_chosen} will earn it, in front of everyone, and set conditions. They are strict, public, and fair, and the quarrel settles into a long, watchful peace.

choices.text: Raise another child of the house too

effects.log: You take another child of the house under your wing, an unfancied one. The quarrel loses half its fuel, and the second child turns out to be the cleverer.

choices.text: Ignore it until the cakes run out

effects.log: You ignore it until the cakes run out. The family finds new topics. The question, unsettled, sits in the corner like a cat.

events.text: {b3_chosen} comes home from the school of fighting arts in the hills with a split lip and a clean conscience. A senior had been bullying a younger pupil, and {b3_chosen} stood in the way. The master of the school writes to praise the courage and ask you to keep your charge from fights. Both letters are on the table. Both are true.

effects.log: You praise the courage, and give {b3_chosen} a good dinner. The younger pupil is a friend of the house for life, and so, strangely, is the senior.

choices.text: Teach a better way to stand in a gap

effects.log: You teach {b3_chosen} how to stand in the way of a blow without taking it. It takes a season, and a great many bruises, and it is worth them.

choices.text: Write to the master with an apology

effects.log: You write to the master with an apology and a gift. The school is satisfied. {b3_chosen} is silent for a month, and then, sweetly, forgives you.

events.text: A suitor comes to your door to ask for {b3_chosen}, with a gift of two goats and a bundle of fine cloth. {b3_chosen} peeks through the shutters, and goes pink, and then white. The suitor is a decent person from a decent family, and the match would be a good one. Nobody has asked {b3_chosen}, and you know it, and so, you suspect, does {b3_chosen}.

effects.log: You ask {b3_chosen} first, in the garden, with the goats looking on. The answer is yes, slowly, and the suitor is let in, and the goats are named.
You say {b3_chosen} is not ready, and offer the goats back. The suitor is gracious, and the family much less so, and {b3_chosen} thanks you in a whisper.
You accept for the house. It is a good match, and a good life, and a long time before {b3_chosen} mentions it, and then only once.

events.text: In a hard winter, {b3_chosen} gives the family's seed-corn to a neighbour without asking. It is a decent thing and a foolish one. When you find out, the barn is a third emptier and {b3_chosen} is standing at the door with chin up, waiting to be scolded. The neighbour's children are, you know, alive.

choices.text: Praise the act, and fix the barn

effects.log: You praise the act, and fix the barn by trading work for grain. The family eats thin all winter, and is proud, and the neighbour sends a goose at midsummer.

choices.text: Scold, and then sit with them

effects.log: You scold, firmly, because the seed-corn was the spring, and then sit with {b3_chosen} for an evening. Both lessons take.

choices.text: Tell the neighbour to return it

effects.log: You tell the neighbour to return it. They do, ashamed, and {b3_chosen} is crushed. The barn is full again, and the house a good deal poorer in another way.

events.text: The village holds its games at midsummer, and {b3_chosen} enters the footrace, the archery, and the long song. They place third, fourth, and first. The song is the one they do not expect to win, and when they stand up to sing it, the whole field goes silent in a way that is not courtesy. You find that you are holding your breath, and so is the old judge.

effects.log: You applaud first, and loudly, before anyone else dares. The field joins, and {b3_chosen}, scarlet, takes a bow that is partly a flee.

choices.text: Say nothing, but wipe your eyes

effects.log: You say nothing, but wipe your eyes. {b3_chosen} sees, and later says it was the best part, better than the prize.

choices.text: Ask what the song was about

effects.log: You ask what the song was about. {b3_chosen} explains, in a rush, and it turns out to be about you, and you spend the evening not knowing where to look.

events.text: {b3_chosen} comes to you in the lean season and asks, quite calmly, to be sent to a good school in a distant town. It would take the house's savings. It would take {b3_chosen} away for four years. They have already looked into the cost, and have written the sum on a slip, in your own handwriting style. You are, you realise, being asked to let go in good order.

choices.text: Send them, and pay for all of it

effects.log: You send them with the whole sum. The house is thin for four years and bright for forty after. {b3_chosen} writes every month, and the letters get better.

choices.text: Send them, but on a half scholarship

effects.log: You send them on a half scholarship, which means writing to a great many people. It works, and {b3_chosen} knows how it worked, and never forgets who wrote.

choices.text: Ask them to wait a year

effects.log: You ask them to wait a year. {b3_chosen} does, with a bearing so even that it is almost an accusation, and goes the year after with your blessing.

events.text: Years on, {b3_chosen} comes home from somewhere larger with a word for you: a position offered in the capital, with a good wage, and a request that you come too. Your hands are the size of the house, your habits the size of the fields. You see {b3_chosen} knows both, and has come anyway, and is standing very straight indeed.

effects.log: You say yes, and go. The capital is loud and strange, and you sleep badly for a year, and wake one morning at home in it.

choices.text: Say no, and wave them off

effects.log: You say no, and wave them off at the gate. {b3_chosen} promises to write, and does, and comes back every harvest, and you keep a chair for them.

choices.text: Say yes for a season, only

effects.log: You say yes for a season, only, and go back in the spring. {b3_chosen} understands, and cries, and the capital learns to expect your visits.

events.text: You take {b3_pet} up to the high stone at midsummer, the way the old stories say. The herders have followed at a respectful distance, with their hats in their hands. The wind drops. {b3_pet} stands on the stone and looks out at the whole valley, and the valley, with the odd intelligence of valleys, seems to look back. Nobody breathes.

choices.text: Say a few words to the valley

effects.log: You say a few words to the valley, simple ones. Somewhere a sheep bleats, and a bird answers, and a quiet settles that feels like a signature.
You kneel beside {b3_pet} and say nothing. The herders, behind you, kneel too, a rustle like grass in the wind.
You hold {b3_pet} close, as you always have, and let the stories take care of themselves. Whatever the valley is deciding, it can decide around the two of you.

events.text: By the next market day the herders are calling {b3_pet} by a new name, a grand one, in the old dialect, and people from the other side of the river come to see. They bring honey, wool, small bells. You find yourself the keeper of something that belongs, now, to everyone. {b3_pet} accepts the gifts, one by one, with the dignity of a creature who knows it is a legend.

choices.text: Share the gifts among the poor

effects.log: You share the gifts among the poor, with the herders' help. {b3_pet} watches, and seems, in some way, to approve.

choices.text: Keep the bells and the wool

effects.log: You keep the bells and the wool, and hang the bells on the beam. When the wind blows, the whole house rings, and you cannot be unhappy in it.
You politely ask them to stop. They bow, and obey, and the gifts become a quiet custom of leaving things at the stone, unseen.

events.text: An old herder, one of the keepers of the world's stories, comes to your door with a cup of strong tea and a look of great gravity. She says that a beast taken up to the stone is a beast that will remember, and that it will outlive you, and that you ought to say now what you would like it to remember. She sits, with the tea, and waits.

effects.log: You say: that you loved it, plainly. The herder writes it in a book of knots, with a long, careful thumb, and says that this, at least, will be kept.

choices.text: Say: that I was a fair keeper

effects.log: You say: that you were a fair keeper, no more, no less. The herder nods. It is the sort of statement a beast can carry for a thousand years.

choices.text: Say: let it forget me, and be free

effects.log: You say: let it forget you, and be free. The herder stops, and puts down the pen, and for a long moment says nothing at all.

events.text: On the way down from the stone, {b3_pet} stops, and turns, and puts its forehead against yours. It is an old gesture, from before the stories. Behind you, a child who has followed you asks in a whisper whether {b3_pet} is a god now. You say no, and hear yourself say it: it is exactly what it was, and now everyone can see it.

choices.text: Press back, and close your eyes

effects.log: You press back, and close your eyes. For a moment you are the whole valley. Then it is only a forehead, and warmth, and a beast who is a friend.

choices.text: Tell the child what it was before

effects.log: You tell the child what {b3_pet} was before: a small wet thing in a basket, who ate your best shoe. The child laughs, and is never afraid of the stone again.

choices.text: Say nothing, and walk on together

effects.log: You say nothing, and walk on together. It is the right silence. The child falls behind, and is allowed to.

events.text: The other great beasts of the world hear about {b3_pet}. At dusk, from the dark of the hills, a long low call goes up, and is answered from the far side of the river, and then from the marsh, and then, very far, from somewhere you have never been. {b3_pet} lifts its head. Then it answers, and the whole valley rings. It is, you realise, being welcomed.

choices.text: Stay and listen to the whole chorus

effects.log: You stay and listen to the whole chorus, until it fades into the stars. You will never forget it. You will never be able to describe it.

choices.text: Let {b3_pet} go to them for a night

effects.log: You let {b3_pet} go to them for a night. It returns at dawn smelling of unfamiliar grass, and sleeps for a day with its paws twitching.

choices.text: Call it back to your side

effects.log: You call it back to your side. It comes, with a soft sound of reproach, and lies at your feet. The valley goes quiet. You are not sure you were right.

events.text: The village elders hold a small ceremony at the stone. They place a ring of flowers around the base, and a bowl of milk, and read out a long list of names: the keepers of the great beasts of this world, going back eleven generations. At the end of the list there is a space. They look at you. They ask, rather shyly, whether they may write your name, and {b3_pet}'s, in it.

effects.log: You let them write both names, side by side. The clerk's hand shakes. The ink dries. The list is longer by two, and the world is a little more as it should be.
You ask them to write only {b3_pet}'s. They do, and under it, quietly, a small line in the margin: with the one who brought it.

choices.text: Add the keeper of the first beast

effects.log: You ask them to add the name of the keeper of the first beast, who was forgotten. The elders blink, and look it up, and write it, with tears.

events.text: You wake in the night to find {b3_pet} sitting at the foot of your bed, watching you, as it did when it was small. It is far larger now, and the roof beam creaks. It does not seem to want anything. It seems only to be keeping you company in the plain way of beasts who have decided that someone is theirs. You sit up, and put out a hand.

choices.text: Lay your head on its flank

effects.log: You lay your head on its flank, and listen to the huge slow engine of its breath. You sleep like a child, and in the morning you do not say why you are smiling.
You talk to it until dawn, about everything: the harvest, the old days, what you are afraid of. It does not answer, and listens, and that is the point.
You fall asleep sitting up, one hand on its ear. In the morning there is a crick in your neck and a smell of wet fur and an extraordinary calm.

events.text: A traveller on the road, a stranger from beyond the hills, stops at the stone and asks the herders about the great beast that is said to be in the valley. They describe {b3_pet}. They describe the gifts, the ceremony, the stories. The traveller listens and then asks, curiously, what the beast was like before. The herders look at you. It seems that only you know.

effects.log: You tell them, truthfully: loud, vain, afraid of ducks. The herders are enchanted, and the traveller writes it all down and takes it over the hills.

choices.text: Say it was always like this

effects.log: You say it was always like this. It is a little lie, and a gift, and it settles, over the years, into a truth.

choices.text: Say it was only a friend

effects.log: You say it was only a friend. The traveller, who has an ear for these things, nods slowly, and stays for supper.

events.text: On the high road a great beast of the hills stands in your way. It does not threaten. It looks at you for a long time, and the herders who follow at a distance tell you it has never let a stranger near. Then it lowers its head, as to someone it has known. You have never seen it before in your life. You are quite sure of this. The beast seems less so.

choices.text: Stay still, and let it look

effects.log: You stay still, and let it look. It sniffs your sleeve, your hand, your boot, and then sighs, exactly as an old dog sighs at an expected visitor.
You speak to it, quietly, the way you speak to a nervous horse. It listens to every word, and its ears move as if they were being read to.
You back away, and go round by the lower path. It watches you the whole way, and does not follow, and does not look surprised.

events.text: Months later, the great beast is waiting on the same bend of the road, and this time it falls into step beside you without a sound. The herders mutter, and keep a distance. It walks you to the next village and then stops, as if at a boundary only it can see. It looks back once. You have the odd sense of having been escorted.

effects.log: You thank it, aloud, with a small bow. It huffs, and turns, and goes back up the hill. The herders watching decide, privately, that you are lucky.

choices.text: Leave a gift at the boundary

effects.log: You leave a gift at the boundary, a loaf and a ribbon. The next morning the loaf is gone, and the ribbon is tied to a post with a perfect knot.

events.text: An old herder in the next village sits you down by the fire, and tells you, without ceremony, that the great beast was once a companion to a person of the valley, long ago, a keeper who loved it and brought it to the stone. She says it has been looking for something for centuries. She says she does not know what. She says it has found you, and you must make of that what you will.

choices.text: Ask what the keeper was like

effects.log: You ask what the keeper was like. She tells you, in a low voice, and as she talks you understand that you have never heard of this person, and miss them anyway.
You say it is a coincidence. She shrugs, pours you more tea, and says that is a perfectly good thing to say, and that the beast will not mind.

choices.text: Go back to the hill alone

effects.log: You go back to the hill alone, at dawn, and sit where the beast sits. It comes, and lies down, and for a long time you both look at the valley.

events.text: A herder's child comes to your door to say that the great beast has had a cub, an impossible thing, as there is only one of its kind, and brings it down to the village to be seen. The cub is a ball of fur and indignation. It bites your sleeve and will not let go. The great beast, on the hill, watches. The herder's child is thrilled and terrified.

effects.log: You hold the cub, gently, and it stops biting and falls asleep on your arm. The great beast, on the hill, lowers its head.

choices.text: Take the cub back up the hill

effects.log: You carry the cub back up the hill yourself. The great beast takes it from you with enormous delicacy, and looks at you for a long time.

choices.text: Let the child take it back

effects.log: You let the child take it back. It goes, in a heap, with a good deal of squeaking, and nobody is bitten.

events.text: The cub, grown, comes down from the hills on its own one winter evening and sits outside your door. It is not tame, and not wild. It has a look that says it has been told about you. You open the door. It does not come in. It lies down across the threshold, like a small hill, and snow begins to cover it, and you cover it with a rug.

choices.text: Sit up with it by the door

effects.log: You sit up with it by the door all night. In the morning the snow is deep and the cub is warm, and walks away with a dignity that makes you laugh.

choices.text: Leave out a dish of milk

effects.log: You leave out a dish of milk and a rug. In the morning the dish is polished clean and the rug has become a sort of nest.

events.text: The great beast has grown old, the herders say, and the cub has grown into something nobody quite expected. Today the two of them stand together on the high stone, side by side, and the valley seems to settle. The old herder tells you the beast will go to the stone to die, soon. She asks, with a face that has seen everything, whether you would like to be there.

effects.log: You go to the stone, at dusk. The old beast lies down, the cub beside it, and you sit with them both until the stars come out. It is the most peaceful thing you have ever seen.
You send flowers and stay away. It is cowardice, and respect, and you spend the evening at your window, looking at the hill, where something is happening that is not for you.

events.text: At the autumn fair a storyteller tells of the great beast of the valley, and how it was once a companion to a person who brought it to the stone. The crowd knows the story by heart, and mouths along. When the tale reaches its end, the teller bows, and looks straight at you, as if to ask whether you had known the person. You have never heard the name.

effects.log: You ask the teller for more. There is a good deal, of loyalty and of a long wait, and you listen to every word with a feeling you cannot place.

choices.text: Put a coin in the teller's bowl

effects.log: You put a coin in the teller's bowl, and the teller hesitates over it, and then bows lower than the coin deserves.
You slip away before the end, with a lump in your throat you cannot explain. Your feet take you up the hill road in the dark.

events.text: Hunters from a faraway town have come for the great beast, with nets and a cart, and are camped at the foot of the hill. Some in the village mutter that it would bring money to the valley. Others say it is the valley. You are asked, by both sides, as a person with a reputation for fairness, to say what is to be done.

ok.log: You face the hunters down, in the open, with half the village behind you. They sulk, and pack, and are gone by dawn, and the beast, on the hill, watches them out of sight.

fail.log: The hunters laugh at you, and it takes the whole village, in the end, to send them off. The beast is untouched. You are not.

choices.text: Buy them off with a good story

effects.log: You buy them off with a good story: of a far larger beast, in a far bigger valley. They believe it, and go, and you do not feel good about it.
You climb the hill and warn the beast to hide. It looks at you with something very like amusement, and goes about its business as before. The hunters never find it.
